title: Vibecoding and security
author: VolatilityLoverr
selftext:
I see a lot of posts about you guys making new games and apps and many times the OP says that they don't know much about coding,then what about security? How can you build an app if you know how to properly secure your work .

Literally the same thing applies to me , thinking about building multiplayer games ,apps with chats/video calls . All of this makes me scared to even try building them ,100% it can easily be picked apart if everything is coded by AI and we know 0 about cybersecurity

comments.author: Ohgood9002
comments.body: Anything can be easily picked apart now period. Cybersecurity is on the ropes

replies.author: mallcopsarebastards
replies.body: a lot of people in here acting like they have the first clue what they're talking about. I'm a 20yr app/cloud sec engineer, I spent 8 years at a FAANG now I lead a red team at an AI sec startup. We're using frontier claude/gpt family models every single day in our workflows, and I can tell you with high confidence that they're nowhere near being able to do this work without human, SME guidance.

replies.body: yes, pentesting requires a good analisis and the AI basically tries to brute-force everything until find something

replies.author: Kindly_Life_947
replies.body: being a software engineer includes cybersecurity in the training. But I can say with confidense that absolutely nobody thinks about it in game development unless its related to payments etc

comments.author: Sencha-Games
comments.body:
Where you have gaps in understanding, why don't you just ask Claude?

If you're trying to make a multiplayer game and you want to prevent cheating, well that's a game of whack-a-mole. Developers have been trying to prevent it for decades and cheaters find interesting new ways to circumvent it.

The fundamentals are to keep everything that matters server authoritative and verify the integrity of the player's (and the server's, if you're allowing self hosting) binary.

comments.author: Old-Moment-5297
comments.body: You can ask AI about it... spend some time learning. I've done several tools for my workplace vibecoding them and where the most secure that they've seen, hardly any issue during VAPT. Of course I used multiple prompts and test to harden the code, not a huge task.

comments.author: Figure_431
comments.body:
LLMs are usually fine with it but by time, they forget what it is fixed. 
I recommend asking LLM to do a full security check before every release and never talk LLMs like "never suggest me something like this". The more negative context you push, the more it lose ability to keep in order. since every message you write actually turned into a call with data "skills + memory + agent.md + your previous messages + AI previous answers". 
so sometimes you talk very negative cause to ignore something. therefore you should read the security check reports.

IE:
* You: Never save user password without salting
* LLM: yeah bla bla bla bla. very long message here.
You: don't do it. give me yes or no.

A few minutes later:
* you : do security check.

LLM:
* ....
* ...
- I ignored whether password is salted since you said I should not do it.
* ....


Security doesn't mean only make sure no one reach your servers or hack you. it's also important how and what you keep. For example, you have to get some consent if you save emails or make sure your users are not under some threshold depending on the region.

But at the end, LLM is a tool that runs other small programs which we call tools. From you to output, there is a looong way. Having a basic understanding of code is always good. Otherwise everything is often fine.

comments.author: Good-Acanthaceae-136
comments.body: What people don't know about, they don't think about. The majority here probably couldn't even tell you what a draw call is let alone be thinking about security. You're mainly just going to get people saying ask AI to make it more secure.

comments.author: taosecurity
comments.body:
I've worked in security almost 30 years. The LLM knows more about code security than I ever will, because I've worked in incident detection, response, and forensics. 

Fun fact -- I know several models were trained on my books because I'm part of the author class action lawsuit. So, you could ask a model to implement a network security monitoring program in my style and it would know.

comments.author: Negative-Tear5402
comments.body:
I think something worth pursuing is, there's a lot of github open source projects that address your problems. People release these skeletons of projects that have the security part built (at least the foundation) and they leave it up to you to build the rest to match your project.

Maybe finding a reputable one and then hooking up an AI to it to understand the project and explain how to expand outwards would be the way to go?

comments.author: novashiftinteractVN
comments.body: Your AI can enforce your code security but you have to ask for it. for example a simple thing is to mention it to apply a review for the owasp top 10 (if you have a website or server it helps a lot)

comments.author: AnAnnouncer
comments.body: If you don't have at least some background in hosting services exposed to the Internet, then best not to make a multiplayer game in the first place. Singleplayer games can have spaghetti code riddled with vulnerabilities, but it wouldn't matter since the binary is self-contained and doesn't talk to the Internet anyway. But if it's something that touches the network, yes, you've got to know what you're doing.

comments.author: WardedDruid
comments.body:
I use skills that test the security of whatever it is I'm working on.  The skill tests the program and spits out a summary of any issues it has found.  I tell it to fix it, and then I ask for directions on how to test if the fix was actually put in place.

I use 2-3 different skills, and then I use claude and codex to run the skills separately to try and cover as many gaps as possible.

My largest project, I actually sent it to a human developer and paid them to check the system.   The only security issue they uncovered was from abandoned 2fa I had planned in the early stages and then decided against.  There wasn't any real way for anyone to get into the program that way, but I removed it to clean up the code and get rid of something I wasn't going to use any more.

The testing takes 2-3 times longer than the building, but is so worth it.
